463.title: Bigger barns (Luke 12:13–21)
463.hook: a rich man plans his retirement and dies that night
463.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich fool at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: private property is real, but its use is meant to serve the common good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman in the crowd blessed his mother, and he blessed everyone who keeps the word. Your line was hear and keep it. Which word did you keep? Day four hundred sixty-three, a new week.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: Master, tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. It's the tone of siblings across a lawyer's table after a funeral. Jesus refuses to be the judge. Who made me a divider over you? Then he turns to the crowd and says: beware of all covetousness, because a man's life does not consist in the abundance of things he possesses. And he tells them a story about a farmer whose year went very, very well. Today, the bigger barns.
screen: `TELL MY BROTHER TO SPLIT IT.` → `WHO MADE ME A DIVIDER?` → `A FARMER'S VERY GOOD YEAR.`

segments.voice: A rich man's land brings in a huge harvest. His problem is a good one to have: nowhere to put it all. So he talks to himself, and Luke lets us listen. What shall I do? I know. I will pull down my barns and build greater, and store everything there. And I'll say to my soul: soul, you have plenty laid up for many years, take your rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself. Notice who he's talking to. Only himself. My crops, my barns, my goods, my soul. Nobody else is in the room. Not his workers, not his neighbors, not the hungry, not God. Then God speaks into the room: "Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?" This night. Not in many years. Tonight. The man planned a retirement and didn't get an evening. And the question cuts back to the brothers fighting at the start: whose will it all be? Jesus finishes: so is he that lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. Notice he's not called a fool for having a good harvest or for planning ahead. Joseph stored grain in Egypt and saved lives. The man is a fool because the harvest only ever went into barns. Saint Basil the Great, preaching on this parable, put it bluntly: the extra bread you store belongs to the hungry, and the shoes rotting in your closet belong to someone barefoot. The Catechism calls this the universal destination of goods: what we own is meant, in the end, to serve everyone.
screen: `A HARVEST WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · `MY CROPS, MY BARNS, MY SOUL.` · `RICH TOWARD GOD.` · `BASIL: THE EXTRA BREAD IS THEIRS.` · then, large: `THOU FOOL, THIS NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away something stored up. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own barns: a garage, a shelf, a drawer, a savings account, a pile of things kept for someday. Walk through it in your mind slowly. Notice one thing that you aren't using and somebody else could. A set of tools, a book, a sum of money, an hour you could give. Decide where it's going and when, today if you can. If you pray, ask to be rich toward God. The bell holds the time.
Bigger barns. The rich farmer's plan to store everything for himself, and God's answer: this night your soul is required of you. Today's word.
Your line: this night. Today, get one stored-up thing out of your barn and into someone's hands before you go to sleep. Day four hundred sixty-three.

464.title: Consider the lilies (Luke 12:22–34)
464.hook: the ravens don't sow, the lilies don't spin
464.howItsDone: Catholics hear this teaching on anxiety in the Gospel readings at Mass, and some pray with it when they speak of trusting God's providence, his care for all he has made.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farmer built bigger barns and didn't get one evening to enjoy them. Your line was this night. What did you give away? Day four hundred sixty-four.

Two in the morning, and the ceiling has become very interesting. Rent, a test result, a child who hasn't texted back, the thing said at work that can't be unsaid. Worry doesn't keep office hours. Right after the story of the rich man and his barns, Jesus turns to his own disciples, people who have no barns at all, and talks about exactly this. He doesn't give them a budget. He tells them to look at two things: a bird and a flower. Today, the ravens and the lilies.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `WORRY KEEPS NO OFFICE HOURS.` → `A BIRD AND A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Jesus says: be not solicitous for your life, what you'll eat, or for your body, what you'll wear. Solicitous is the Douay's word for anxious. Then the first picture: "Consider the ravens, for they sow not, neither do they reap, neither have they storehouse nor barn, and God feedeth them." No barn. That's a pointed word right after yesterday. And Luke says ravens, where Matthew says simply the birds of the air. The raven was a scavenger, a noisy black bird, and the Law of Moses listed it among the birds not to be eaten. Not a pretty bird. God feeds it anyway. Then the second picture: "Consider the lilies, how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin." Spinning thread was daily work, the way people made cloth. The lilies make nothing, and yet Solomon in all his glory wasn't dressed like one of them. Which flower did Jesus mean? The text doesn't say, and nobody knows for sure. Readers have guessed anemones, irises and others. Then the punch line: which of you, by taking thought, can add to his stature one cubit? Worry doesn't add anything. And then a tender line: fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you a kingdom. So sell what you have, give alms, and make purses that don't wear out. Because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Consider is the key word. It means look closely, study, take your time. Jesus doesn't argue people out of worry. He asks them to look at something alive and let it teach them.
screen: `BE NOT SOLICITOUS: DON'T BE ANXIOUS.` · `RAVENS: NO STOREHOUSE, NO BARN.` · `LILIES: THEY NEITHER LABOR NOR SPIN.` · `FEAR NOT, LITTLE FLOCK.` · then, large: `CONSIDER THE LILIES, HOW THEY GROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a flower and stop worrying. If you can, find a real one: a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a picture on your phone if that's all you have. Settle, and breathe. Now consider it, the way Jesus said: slowly. The color at the center. The way the petals are folded. How it's simply being what it is. When a worry walks in, notice it, and gently bring your eyes back to the flower. If you pray, let it remind you who clothes it. The bell holds the time.
Consider the lilies. Jesus' cure for anxiety: look closely at ravens with no barns and flowers that never spin, and remember who feeds and clothes them. Today's word.
Your line: consider the lilies. Today, when worry starts to spin, stop and look closely at one living thing for ten seconds. Day four hundred sixty-four.

465.title: One more year (Luke 13:6–9)
465.hook: a fruitless fig tree gets another year of digging and dung
465.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the fig tree at Mass during Lent in the year of Luke's Gospel, a season the Church treats as a time of repentance and of God's patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ravens with no barns and lilies that never spin. Your line was consider the lilies. What did you look at closely? Day four hundred sixty-five.

A tomato plant that never sets fruit. The rosebush that just sits there, green and stubborn, year after year. At some point you stand over it with the shovel and decide: that's it, it's coming out, and something useful is going in. Jesus tells a story about exactly that moment: an owner, a fig tree, and a gardener who asks for one thing before the shovel comes down. It's four verses long. Today, one more year.
screen: `THE PLANT THAT NEVER FRUITS.` → `STANDING THERE WITH THE SHOVEL.` → `A GARDENER ASKS FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The setting matters. Just before this, people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate while offering sacrifice, and Jesus mentions eighteen people crushed when a tower fell at Siloam. Were they worse sinners than everyone else? No, he says, but unless you repent, you'll all likewise perish. It's a warning. Then he tells this parable. A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. For three years he's come looking for figs and found none. So he tells the dresser of the vineyard: cut it down. Why should it take up the ground? The dresser answers: "Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig about it, and dung it." If it bears fruit, good. If not, then after that you can cut it down. And that's where the story stops. Luke never tells us what happened to the tree. The parable is left open, like a door, and the listener is standing in it. Look at what the gardener does. He doesn't just ask for time. He promises work: dig around the roots, so water can reach them, and spread manure, the least glamorous job in any garden. Mercy here isn't looking the other way. It's getting your hands dirty for something that hasn't earned it. Some Christian readers, Catholic preachers among them, have heard the owner as the Father, and the gardener as Christ, who pleads for more time and does the digging himself. Others hear it more simply: God is patient, and patience has a deadline. Both readings keep the warning and the mercy together. The tree still needs to bear fruit. But it gets another year, and somebody to tend it.
screen: `THE TOWER AT SILOAM.` · `THREE YEARS, NO FIGS.` · `DIG ABOUT IT, AND DUNG IT.` · `THE STORY ENDS OPEN.` · then, large: `LET IT ALONE THIS YEAR ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone more time. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you're close to giving up on. A friend who keeps canceling. A coworker who hasn't changed. A family member, or maybe yourself. Picture them as that fig tree, and you standing there with the shovel. Now picture the gardener's choice: one more year, and some digging. What would digging around their roots look like? A conversation, a little help, a little less judgment. Pick one small thing. If you pray, pray for them. The bell holds the time.
One more year. The gardener's plea for a fruitless fig tree: time, digging and manure before anyone cuts it down. Today's word.
Your line: let it alone this year. Today, put the shovel down for one person, and do one small thing to help them grow. Day four hundred sixty-five.

466.title: The bent woman (Luke 13:10–17)
466.hook: eighteen years bent over, healed on the sabbath, and she stands straight
466.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the sick at Mass and through the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, in which the priest lays hands on the sick person, as Jesus did here.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gardener begged one more year for a fig tree with no figs. Your line was let it alone this year. Who did you give more time? Day four hundred sixty-six.

Try this for a moment, wherever you are. Let your head drop and your back curl until you're looking at the floor. Stay there. You can see feet, and dust, and the hem of other people's clothes. You can't see a face unless someone bends down to you. Now imagine that for eighteen years. Going to the market like that. Going to the synagogue like that. Luke says there was a woman who lived exactly this way, and one sabbath Jesus was teaching in her synagogue. Today, the bent woman.
screen: `LOOK AT THE FLOOR. STAY THERE.` → `EIGHTEEN YEARS OF FEET AND DUST.` → `ONE SABBATH IN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Luke describes her carefully: "there was a woman, who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years: and she was bent down, neither could she look upwards at all." Notice she doesn't ask for anything. Luke only says she was there. Jesus sees her and calls her over. He says: "Woman, thou art delivered from thy infirmity." He lays his hands on her, and immediately she's made straight, and she glorifies God. Then a complication. The ruler of the synagogue is indignant, because it's the sabbath, and he tells the crowd: there are six days for work. Come and be healed on those, not on the sabbath. It's worth being fair to him. Keeping the sabbath holy was, and is, a deep act of faithfulness for Jews, and he's trying to protect it. Jesus answers from inside that same faithfulness. Every one of you, he says, unties his ox or his donkey on the sabbath and leads it to water. And this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound these eighteen years, shouldn't she be untied on the sabbath day? Daughter of Abraham. The title gives her back her full place among God's people. The sabbath, in Jesus' reading, is exactly the day for setting someone free. Luke ends with the crowd rejoicing at all the glorious things he was doing. Eighteen years of looking at the floor, and then she stood up.
screen: `EIGHTEEN YEARS, BENT DOWN.` · `WOMAN, THOU ART DELIVERED.` · `THE OX UNTIED ON THE SABBATH.` · `A DAUGHTER OF ABRAHAM.` · then, large: `SHE WAS MADE STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand up straight and give thanks. If you're able, stand. If not, sit tall. Start bent: let your head drop and your shoulders curl. Breathe there a moment. Then, slowly, unroll your spine one piece at a time, until your head rises and you're looking straight ahead. Feel your chest open. Breathe into it. Think of one thing you're grateful for today. If you pray, give thanks to God the way she did. If you don't, simply let yourself feel glad to be upright. The bell holds the time.
The bent woman. Eighteen years unable to look up, healed by Jesus on the sabbath and called a daughter of Abraham. Today's word.
Your line: she stood up. Today, every time you notice yourself hunched over a screen, stand up straight, look up, and say thanks. Day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: The hen and her chicks (Luke 13:31–35)
467.hook: Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem like a hen gathers her brood
467.howItsDone: Catholics pray for their cities in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and many parishes hold processions or vigils through their neighborhoods; Psalm 91, with its shelter under God's wings, is prayed at Night Prayer on Sundays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman bent over for eighteen years was made straight on the sabbath. Your line was she stood up. Did you look up today? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

If you've ever watched a mother hen when a hawk's shadow crosses the yard, you've seen something fast. She calls with a sharp cluck, the chicks run to her, and she spreads her wings and crouches so they disappear underneath. All you see is one puffed-up bird, staring the danger down. Whatever comes now, comes to her first. Jesus is on his long road to Jerusalem when some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him. His answer starts with a fox and ends with a hen. Today, the hen and her chicks.
screen: `A HAWK'S SHADOW ON THE YARD.` → `THE CHICKS VANISH UNDER HER.` → `A FOX, THEN A HEN.`

segments.voice: First, notice who warns him. Some Pharisees come and say: get out of here, Herod wants to kill you. Not every Pharisee in the Gospels is an opponent, and these seem to be trying to protect him. Jesus answers: go and tell that fox, today and tomorrow I cast out devils and heal, and on the third day I'm finished. He won't be rushed by a fox. Then his voice turns, and he speaks to a city that isn't there. "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent to thee, how often would I have gathered thy children as the bird doth her brood under her wings, and thou wouldest not?" The Douay says bird. The Greek word can mean any bird, but it was the usual word for a hen, and English Bibles have long said hen. Think about the picture Jesus chose. Not a lion or an eagle, which kings liked. A hen. A barnyard mother with nothing to fight with but her own body. Herod is a fox, and Jesus pictures himself as the hen who stands between the fox and the chicks. The Hebrew scriptures already spoke this way about God: the Psalms ask to be hidden under the shadow of your wings. And notice the words and thou wouldest not. Jesus doesn't force the gathering. A hen can call; she can't make a chick run. There's grief in this line, not anger. Catholic writers have long loved the image. Saint Anselm wrote a prayer calling Jesus our mother, who gathers us under his wings like a hen. It's tender, and strong, and a little surprising.
screen: `PHARISEES WARN HIM ABOUT HEROD.` · `GO AND TELL THAT FOX.` · `JERUSALEM, JERUSALEM.` · `A HEN, NOT AN EAGLE.` · then, large: `AS THE BIRD DOTH HER BROOD UNDER HER WINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your city. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place where you live, close up, at street level. The bus stop. The clinic waiting room. The school gate. The doorway where someone sleeps. Let one part of it come close: a neighborhood that's struggling, a corner where someone was hurt. Picture wings spread over it. If you pray, ask God to gather your city under his wings. If you don't, simply hold it in your attention, with care. The bell holds the time.
The hen and her chicks. Jesus' picture of himself longing to gather Jerusalem under his wings, standing between the fox and the brood. Today's word.
screen: `THE HEN AND HER CHICKS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: under her wings. Today, notice one place in your city that needs sheltering, and do or pray one thing for it. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: The lowest place (Luke 14:7–14)
468.hook: sit at the bottom of the table, and invite those who can't repay
468.carry: invite the ones who can't repay
468.howItsDone: Some Catholic parishes and communities, such as the Catholic Worker and the Community of Sant'Egidio, hold meals where the poor sit at the table as guests, not only as people being served food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hen spread her wings over a city that wouldn't come. Your line was under her wings. What did you shelter? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

A wedding reception, and a seating chart on an easel by the door. Table one, near the couple: family and the best friends. Table twelve, by the kitchen door: the coworkers and the plus-ones nobody's met. Guests find their names, and at least one quietly moves a place card. Jesus is at a dinner on the sabbath, in the house of a leading Pharisee, and he's watching the guests do exactly this: angling for the first seats. So he gives them some advice. Today, the lowest place.
screen: `A SEATING CHART BY THE DOOR.` → `TABLE TWELVE, BY THE KITCHEN.` → `GUESTS ANGLING FOR THE BEST SEATS.`

segments.voice: First, to the guests. Don't grab the top seat, he says. Someone more honored may arrive, and the host will ask you to move, and you'll walk the whole room to the bottom in front of everybody. "But when thou art invited, go, sit down in the lowest place." Then the host may come and say: friend, go up higher, and you'll be honored in front of the whole table. It sounds like good manners, and it is. The Book of Proverbs gives almost the same advice about standing before a king. But Jesus ends with a line that goes past manners: "every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted." Then he turns to the host. When you give a dinner, don't invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives or your rich neighbors, because they'll invite you back, and that's your repayment. Instead: "call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind; And thou shalt be blessed, because they have not wherewith to make thee recompense." That's the harder half. Jesus names the loop himself: you invite me, I invite you, and the account is settled. Jesus says: break the loop. Invite the people who can't pay you back, and let God do the repaying, at the resurrection of the just. The two halves fit together. As a guest, don't measure your worth by your seat. As a host, don't measure your guests by what they can give. So the lowest place isn't a trick for getting promoted. It's a way of sitting at a table where nobody is keeping score.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the lower seat. Settle, and breathe. Think through today's rooms: a meeting, a meal, a line, a group chat, a car. Where would you usually take the better place: the first word, the best chair, the last slice, the credit? Pick one place today where you'll take the lower one instead, on purpose and quietly. Picture yourself doing it. Notice what that's like. If you pray, ask for a humble heart. The bell holds the time.

Your line: invite the ones who can't repay. Today, take one lower seat, and think about who you could invite this month who could never invite you back. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

469.title: The great supper (Luke 14:15–24)
469.hook: the invited make excuses, and the poor, lame and blind are brought in
469.howItsDone: At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest invites the people with words drawn from the Book of Revelation about those called to the supper of the Lamb; some Catholic readers hear the great supper in that invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seating chart, and the lowest place at the table. Your line was invite the ones who can't repay. Who came to mind? Day four hundred sixty-nine, the end of a week.

You've planned a party. You sent the invitations weeks ago, everyone said yes, and you've cooked all day. Then, an hour before, the texts start. So sorry, something came up. Can't make it, rain check? Then another. Then another. You're standing in a kitchen full of food with an empty room. Still at the same dinner as yesterday, a guest says something pious: blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God. And Jesus answers with a story about exactly that kitchen. Today, the great supper.
screen: `THE TEXTS START AN HOUR BEFORE.` → `A KITCHEN FULL OF FOOD.` → `AN EMPTY ROOM.`

segments.voice: A man makes a great supper and invites many. When it's ready, he sends his servant to say: come, all is ready. And they all, Luke says, begin to make excuse. The first: I've bought a farm and I need to go see it. The second: I've bought five yoke of oxen, and I'm going to try them out. The third: I've married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. Some readers notice how thin these sound: who buys a farm before seeing it, or five yoke of oxen before trying them? The host is angry, but he doesn't cancel. He sends the servant into the streets and lanes of the city: bring in the poor, the maimed, the blind and the lame, exactly the guests from yesterday's teaching. The servant comes back: done, and there's still room. So the master says: "Go out into the highways and hedges; and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." Today's line has a hard history. Compel was read, centuries later, as permission to force people into the faith. Saint Augustine, in a bitter fight with the Donatists in North Africa, used this verse to defend pressure from the state. The Church today reads it differently. The Second Vatican Council taught that no one may be forced to embrace the faith against their will. Read inside the story, compel sounds like the host's urgency, not violence: the servant goes out to people on the roadsides who would hardly expect an invitation, and has to insist. And at Mass, just before Communion, the priest holds up the host and says that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed, words drawn from the Book of Revelation.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say yes to one invitation. Settle, and breathe. Think of an invitation you've been dodging: a friend's dinner, a parish event, a call from your mother, a chance to help, an invitation to pray that you keep putting off. Notice the excuse you've been using. Is it a farm you have to see, or something real? Picture yourself saying yes, and showing up. If you pray, you can thank God for the invitations in your life. The bell holds the time.
The great supper. A feast the invited guests skipped with thin excuses, so the host filled his house with the poor and the people on the roads. Today's word.

Your line: compel them to come in. Today, say yes to one invitation. And that's week sixty-seven: bigger barns, the lilies, one more year, the bent woman, the hen, the lowest place, and the great supper. Day four hundred sixty-nine.

what it means: in the story, compel is the host's urgency: people on the roads won't believe they're invited, so the servant insists.
what a scholar hears: Augustine cited this verse (Letter 93, Letter 185) against the Donatists; Vatican II's Dignitatis Humanae teaches no one may be coerced into faith.
